summaries.example: Imagine Maya says, “I am here.” The word “I” means Maya when Maya says it. If Leo says the same sentence, “I” means Leo. A 2D chart can show both facts: one direction shows who is speaking, and the other shows what might happen in different possible worlds. The chart helps us see that “I” changes with the speaker, while the person named by a name usually stays the same.
summaries.summary:
Two-dimensional semantics is a special tool for studying meaning. In simpler systems, a sentence is checked against one situation. In ordinary possible-worlds semantics, philosophers compare many ways the world could be. Two-dimensional semantics adds another role for possibilities. One role can represent the context in which words are used, such as who is speaking and when. The other role can represent a possible situation used to test whether what was said is true.

This is useful for words like “I,” “here,” and “this.” If Maya says “I,” the word refers to Maya. If Leo says it, the word refers to Leo. The rule stays steady even though the person changes. A two-dimensional matrix, or chart, can display these changes. It can also help explain words such as “actually” and “necessarily,” which compare what is true in the real world with what is true in other possible worlds.

Philosophers disagree about how broadly to use this tool. Some use it for special expressions only. Others think it can reveal a deeper part of the meaning of many words, including “water.” Another view uses the framework to explain what people communicate when they are unsure about the meanings or references of words. The framework itself is a formal tool; its philosophical meaning depends on how a theory explains its two dimensions.
key_ideas: Ordinary meaning can depend on both what is being talked about and the situation in which words are used.
The word “I” refers to different people in different conversations, but it refers to the speaker in each conversation.
A two-dimensional chart can place possible contexts on one side and possible situations for checking truth on the other.
Philosophers use this framework for indexicals, words such as “actually” and “necessarily,” and larger questions about meaning and communication.
summaries.why_it_matters: The framework helps us notice that meaning is not always just about the object a word points to. It can also involve who is speaking, where they are, what they already assume, and which possible situation is being considered. This gives philosophers a careful way to study language, truth, possibility, and communication.

important_terms.definition: A formal way to study meaning by checking two different roles for possible situations.
A word such as “I,” “here,” or “this” whose meaning depends partly on the situation in which it is used.
A way things could have been, used by philosophers to compare different possibilities.
A rule or value that tells us what an expression refers to or whether a sentence is true.

questions_to_think_about: What changes when different people say “I”?
Does the word “here” mean the same place in every conversation?
Why might a chart with two directions show more than a chart with one direction?
Can a sentence be true whenever someone says it but still describe something that could have been different?

summaries.example: Suppose a speaker says, “Actually, the team won,” while considering different possible worlds. The sentence is evaluated using a designated world as the actual one, even when the sentence is discussed inside a possibility claim. A two-dimensional matrix can put worlds considered as actual on one axis and worlds used as circumstances of evaluation on the other. The diagonal then compares each world with itself. This helps explain why a claim can be necessary in one formal sense while still seeming contingent: the actual world might have been different.
summaries.summary:
Two-dimensional semantics extends possible-worlds semantics by assigning an expression a value relative to two parameters. The framework is not a single theory with one interpretation. A theorist must specify what the two parameters represent, how values are assigned, and what explanatory work those values perform.

In Kaplan’s restricted semantic theory, one dimension concerns a context of use and the other a circumstance of evaluation. A context can be represented as a centered world containing an agent and a time. The character of an expression maps contexts to contents; its content maps possible worlds to extensions. Thus “I” has a variable character because different speakers use it to refer to themselves, while the content expressed in a particular context is rigid with respect to the person selected. This distinction explains why “I” is not synonymous with a particular name, even when one person utters it.

Two-dimensional matrices make the structure visible. Rows can represent contexts and columns circumstances of evaluation. The diagonal is especially important: for some indexical sentences, it displays a truth-preserving pattern. “I am here,” for example, may be true whenever uttered, although each utterance expresses a contingent proposition. Related 2D systems analyze modal operators such as “actually” and “necessarily.” They can represent claims involving the designated actual world, though the source notes that some nested modal examples require multiple indices rather than only two.

The most ambitious use, generalized 2D semantics, applies the framework to meaning more broadly. Jackson’s empiricist project emphasizes shared reference-fixing dispositions that support classification and communication. Chalmers’s rationalist project emphasizes ideal a prior
key_ideas: Standard possible-worlds semantics models an expression relative to one world at a time; 2D semantics distinguishes two roles for possibilities.
Kaplan’s account separates character, which depends on context, from content, which is evaluated across possible worlds.
A sentence such as “I am here” can be true in every context of utterance while expressing a contingent proposition in each context.
2D modal logic gives formal resources for operators such as “actually” and “necessarily,” although some cases motivate more than two indices.
Generalized 2D semantics tries to connect meaning, a priori reasoning, and possibility, while its empiricist and rationalist versions pursue different goals.
Stalnaker’s metasemantic approach uses 2D matrices to model partial understanding and conversational communication without treating diagonal values as basic meanings.
summaries.why_it_matters: Two-dimensional semantics shows why the meaning of an expression may involve more than its reference in a possible world. It helps separate context, content, modality, knowledge, and communication. It also clarifies a major philosophical disagreement: whether a second dimension is a genuine part of semantic meaning, a tool for explaining how meaning is fixed, or an instrument for modeling a speaker’s limited understanding.

important_terms.definition: A formal semantic framework that assigns values relative to two possible-world parameters rather than one.
An expression whose reference varies with a context of use, such as the speaker, time, or location.
In Kaplan’s framework, the rule connecting a context of use with the content expressed there.
In Kaplan’s framework, the modal content evaluated across possible worlds.
A function from possible worlds to extensions or truth-values; it represents how an expression behaves across possibilities.
The diagonal pattern in a 2D matrix, used to track what happens when a possible world serves both as context and as the situation evaluated.
Knowledge or justification available independently of particular empirical investigation.
An interpretation that uses 2D structures to explain how semantic values are fixed, rather than treating the structures themselves as ordinary meanings.

questions_to_think_about: Why does a standard one-dimensional intension fail to distinguish “I” from a fixed proper name?
How can “I am here” be valid in every context yet express something that could have been false?
What is the difference between a world considered as actual and a world considered as a counterfactual circumstance?
Should a speaker’s hypothetical judgments count as part of meaning, or only as evidence about meaning?
Why might an assertion of a necessary identity still communicate useful empirical information?

summaries.example: Imagine two students using the word “water” in two imagined places. On Earth, the clear liquid in lakes is H2O. On Twin Earth, the same-looking liquid is XYZ. A 2D chart can ask two questions: Which place is being treated as the actual home of the speakers? And, once that is fixed, which substance is being considered in a possible situation? Some philosophers say the chart shows a reference-fixing idea shared by speakers. Others say it shows only what speakers know or assume, not the word’s full meaning.
summaries.summary:
Two-dimensional semantics is a formal framework for representing meaning with two kinds of possible-world information. In ordinary possible-worlds semantics, an expression is evaluated relative to one possible world. Two-dimensional approaches add a second role for worlds. A world may help describe the context in which an expression is used, while another world serves as the situation in which the expression is evaluated.

This distinction matters for indexicals. The word “I” refers to the speaker in each context, but the speaker could have been different in another context. Kaplan describes this with character and content. Character is the rule that links an expression to a context; content is what that expression contributes once the context has fixed a referent. A matrix can display contexts in rows and evaluation worlds in columns. Proper names, descriptions, and indexicals produce different patterns in such a matrix.

The framework also applies to modal operators. An operator like “actually” tells us to evaluate a claim at a designated actual world, even when that claim occurs inside a statement about what is possible. This gives the logic more expressive power, but it can also create surprising results about necessity. Some examples suggest that more than two world indices may be needed for complex modal sentences.

The entry then describes competing broader projects. Generalized 2D semantics tries to use the framework for many expressions and to connect meaning with a priori knowledge and possibility. Jackson’s empiricist interpretation focuses on shared, psychologically useful reference-fixing patterns. Chalmers’s rationalist interpretation focuses on ideal reflection and epistemic possibilities. Stalnaker’s metasemantic interpretation takes a different path: 2D
key_ideas: A one-dimensional theory can describe what an expression refers to in a possible world, but it may miss how the context of use affects reference.
Kaplan’s theory explains indexicals by distinguishing character from content.
A 2D matrix lets us compare worlds as contexts with worlds as situations in which truth is evaluated.
Some philosophers generalize the framework to explain how speakers understand words such as “water,” even when they are ignorant about chemistry.
Jackson emphasizes shared reference-fixing habits and communication; Chalmers emphasizes a priori reasoning and possibility.
Stalnaker uses 2D models to explain what an assertion can communicate when speakers are partly mistaken or ignorant about word meanings.
summaries.why_it_matters: The topic matters because language is shaped both by what words refer to and by how people use and understand them. Two-dimensional models give philosophers a precise way to discuss context, possible situations, uncertainty, assertion, and the difference between literal meaning and communicated information. The competing interpretations also show how one formal tool can support different philosophical explanations.

important_terms.definition: A system for studying meaning by using two kinds of possible situations instead of one.
A context-sensitive expression, such as “I,” “here,” or “that,” whose reference depends on its use.
A possible way the world could be, used for thinking about necessity and possibility.
A representation of how an expression maps situations to objects, properties, or truth-values.
The part of an expression’s meaning that determines what it refers to in a context of use.
A proposed rule for identifying what a word refers to, even when speakers do not know the thing’s deeper nature.
Reasoning or knowledge that does not depend on finding out particular facts through experience.
A theory about what makes an expression have a particular meaning, rather than simply stating that meaning.

questions_to_think_about: If two people say “I,” what stays the same: the word, its rule, or its referent?
Why might “water” have different reference-fixing patterns in Earth and Twin Earth?
Can something be true whenever it is said but still be false in another possible situation?
Is a model of what speakers understand automatically a model of literal meaning?
How can an assertion of an identity teach someone something if the identity is necessary once its names are fixed?
